t: The Aoun (Awn) Family, from Damour to Brooklyn
x: What we found The family was Aoun in Damour. The family says the name became Awn in America ( Family ), and records also wrote it Owen and Aun; Joseph’s death certificate says Owen ( Confirmed ). The Awn story begins in Damour, a coastal village south of Beirut. Damour sits on the Mediterranean coast about eleven miles south of Beirut. When the Aouns left in the summer of 1920, the First World War had only just ended, and Mount Lebanon was recovering from a wartime famine that, by most historians' estimates, killed a large share of its people. In September 1920, as the family crossed into New York State, France was proclaiming the new state of Greater Lebanon under its mandate. This is background, not a record of this family, and the papers do not tell us why Joseph and Assin decided to go. What they do tell us is that they took all eight children with them, a party of ten on third-class tickets by way of Southampton and Quebec, with Joseph about 50 years old and Brooklyn as their destination. That is a lot to stake on a new country.

Owen” was Yusuf al-Khoury Butrus Awn to his own people. Yusuf is the Arabic form of Joseph, Butrus is Peter, and the K. most likely stands for Khoury (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). “Death of a righteous man” Al-Hoda, 17 September 1932, p.3, the local-news headline over Joseph’s death (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader) When Joseph died in Brooklyn on 14 September 1932, the city recorded him as “Joseph K. Owen,” retired, aged 62, the son of Peter and Teresa Owen. The Arabic paper Al-Hoda printed what looks like another man: “Yusuf al-Khoury Butrus Awn,” of Damour (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). He is one person, and the two names fit together. The ship list of 1920 had already written him a third way, Youseuf Aoun, a farmer or traveler of 53. His death certificate says he was born on 21 November 1869, and that he had lived in the United States for 12 years, which fits the family’s arrival in 1920. He died of cardiac failure with a coronary thrombosis and was buried at St. John’s Cemetery on 16 September. Al-Hoda said he died of a heart attack on the Wednesday morning, that the funeral Mass was at Our Lady of Lebanon on Hicks Street, and said that members of the Damour fraternity came (our translation). The Brooklyn Times Union says St. Mary’s Syrian Roman Catholic Church on Hicks Street; we take these to be one church under two names. The same fraternity may show up two years earlier. On the evening of Monday 28 April 1930, the Damouri Fraternity Society met at Columbus Hall and chose its officers, and its treasurer is printed as “Yusuf al-Khoury Awn” (Al-Hoda, 23 May 1930; our translation). It is probably Joseph, since the name matches the one in his notices and he was a Damour man, but nothing on the page says so, and the other Awns elected with him are named without any link to him. If it was him, he was trusted with the Damour men’s money at the age of sixty. One more page may tell us about his own family. In March 1926 the Damour magazine Ash-Shams printed a notice of the death in Brazil of “the late Jibrail,” who had emigrated about 1911, and it condoled his two brothers, “Khawaja Mikhail in Damour and Khawaja Yusuf in New York” (our translation). The notice is addressed to a Mikhail al-Khoury Boutros Awn, and Joseph’s father is Peter (Butrus) on his certificate. So Joseph may have had a brother who stayed in Damour and another who went to Brazil. This is the only record that says so, and no other record names either brother. A second Ash-Shams page, of July 1934, mentions the family of a “late Jibrail al-Khoury Awn” in Brazil, but it names none of Joseph’s family. His wife Assin Aoun was written Essine on the ship list, Aseen in the 1925 census and Affin in one 1932 notice. Her death certificate gives her father as Joseph Segan (Segen; Sajaan in Arabic) and her mother as Susanne, with a family name that reads Nahmir in a hard-to-read hand. She died on Wednesday 16 October 1935 at Bay Ridge Hospital, a widow living at 1047 75th Street, of a ruptured appendix after an emergency appendectomy. Her son John signed for the burial permit. A Mass was said for her at Our Lady of Lebanon on Friday 18 October, the day she was buried at St. John’s, and Al-Hoda called her “the late Assin Yusuf al-Khoury Awn of Damour,” which probably puts her husband’s name after hers, the usual way in these notices. Her age is written four different ways across the records (45, 40, 50 and 52), so her birth year is unknown. Her notice reads like a map of the neighborhood. It names her children and their families, the sons of Habib Aoun (Sajaan, Khalil, Farid, Sa’id and Shaker), a widow, Sofia Ghareeb, and the Aql family. How the Habib Aoun sons were related to Joseph or Assin we do not know. The same undertaker, Jere J. Cronin, Inc., of Atlantic Avenue, handled both Joseph’s and Assin’s funerals. The cemetery’s own burial search says that in June 1961 St. John’s moved Assin and her son George from Section 20 to Section 3, Row C, the row where the same search places Joseph’s own burial, almost thirty years after his funeral. A volunteer’s Find a Grave listing, made in 2016, still shows Assin and George in Section 20 with three other Owens we do not know. Still open Joseph’s birth: the certificate’s age of 62 years, 9 months and 7 days does not fit its own birth date of 21 November 1869, which gives 62 years, 9 months and 24 days. No Damour record has turned up. Joseph’s grave: the cemetery’s search puts his 1932 burial in Section 3, Row C, Graves 39 to 42, and Find a Grave says Grave 4A. Same man, same date, two grave numbers. The 1961 move: why Assin and George were moved, and whether the Section 20 listing on Find a Grave is out of date, is not known. The two sons: the Al-Hoda item of 17 September 1932 says Joseph was buried beside two sons who died young. No record in hand names them. Joseph’s brothers: Mikhail and Jibrail rest on one Ash-Shams page. Assin’s parents’ names and her age are our best readings of faint writing. Family memory: why they left Damour, what the voyage was like, or what Joseph and Assin were like. If you know, please tell Sarah. Questions for the family Does anyone remember Joseph or Assin, or stories about them? Does anyone know about two children who died young and are buried with Joseph? Does anyone know why Assin and George were moved at St. John’s in 1961? Does anyone know who Mikhail and Jibrail were, or who Michal Malleut, the uncle named on the 1920 ship list, was? Who were the sons of Habib Aoun named in Assin’s notice? Does anyone remember Esther, or a letter from Lebanon? What we found The 1920 ship list shows eight children, but the Arabic death notices of 1930 and 1935 name a ninth, Esther, who stayed in Lebanon ( Confirmed ; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). Eight on the ship, one who stayed Joseph and Assin had nine children. Eight crossed together in 1920, from Nassib, the oldest of the eight ( Probable , going by the ages on the ship list), to Anthony, the youngest on the ship. The ninth, Esther (we do not know her age, so she may have been older than some of the eight), stayed in Lebanon, married there, and died in Beirut in 1961 ( Confirmed : the 1920 manifest, the Arabic death notices of 1930 and 1935, and a 1961 Caravan notice). Two of the brothers died young. Nassib died on 2 October 1924 of pneumonia and tuberculosis, and George drowned in a boat accident on 27 July 1930 ( Confirmed : the Arabic papers, our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader, and the New York papers; no death certificate has been found). Family stories say one brother drowned and another died after surgery on his arm; the records bear out the drowning, but not the surgery ( Family ). About 1897 Nassib born 16 Oct 1899 Mathilde born 2 Oct 1924 Nassib dies 27 Jul 1930 George drowns Before 29 Jan 1961 Esther dies in Beirut The details: records, spellings and open questions The children are listed here from oldest to youngest, with Esther last because we do not know her age: Nassib (born about 1897), written Nessil on the 1920 manifest and Nassib K. Owen on his death certificate. The age (27), parents and address fit, so it is Probable that they are the same man, and the Arabic notices write his name Nassib, which suggests Nessil was a misreading. He was a printer. He died at 6:30 on the evening of Thursday 2 October 1924 at the family home, 37 Tompkins Place, with prayers on Sunday 5 October at 2 p.m. at Our Lady of Lebanon, and was buried at St. John’s Cemetery that day. The cause was broncho-pneumonia (seven days), with pulmonary tuberculosis (five months) contributing ( Confirmed : NYC death certificate; Mira’at al-Gharb and Al-Hoda, 3 October 1924, p. 2). The notice says he was from Damour (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). Koury, age 88, died in March 1994 (Asbury Park Press index and her Social Security file). That fits Theresa's birth year and her married name, so it is Probable that she is Anthony's sister. Where she died is not confirmed: the newspaper index says Berkeley Township, New Jersey, but her Social Security file points to Staten Island. George (born about 1907 to 1909). He was at home in the 1925 state census (age 18) and the 1930 census (age 21, a manager in ladies’ apparel), both in the Owen household ( Probable that he is the Georges on the manifest). George drowned on Sunday 27 July 1930 in a boat accident (one account says a canoe) with a friend ( Confirmed ). His funeral was on Wednesday 30 July at 2 p.m. at Our Lady of Lebanon, 295 Hicks Street ( Confirmed : Mira’at al-Gharb, 28 to 30 July; Al-Hoda, 29 and 30 July; As-Sayeh, 31 July 1930; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). Find a Grave lists a George Owen at St. John’s Cemetery, Section 20, Row S, Grave 207 (memorial 168999663; Probable that this is George, a pointer only). Two things are still open. The papers do not agree on where it happened: the New York papers point to Long Island, and one Arabic paper (Ash-Shams, September 1930) says a lake in Rhode Island, so we say only that he drowned. And his age is 24 in the notices, 21 in the census and 22 in Ash-Shams. One notice may suggest he was engaged to be married; we have not confirmed this, and it is a question for the family. He is not named in his parents’ 1932 and 1935 notices, which makes sense: he had died before either. The documents behind this 2 documents Document 135 George's funeral notice, 30 July 1930 Document 136 George's grave listing (Find a Grave) Mitchell (born 4 July 1909). Elias (Louis) (born 3 May 1912). Louis is the name the 1930 census, his 1937 marriage certificate and the newspaper notices use; the Arabic notices give both names for the same man ( Confirmed ). Anthony (born 6 March 1914), who married Helen Saydah. Esther (birth year not known), who stayed in Lebanon and married there, later Mrs. Ayoub. See her story below. Family stories (told by Jackie) say that two of Anthony’s brothers died young: one drowned, and one died of peritonitis after surgery on his arm. The records now bear out the first half. George drowned in July 1930, and Nassib died in October 1924 ( Confirmed ). Nassib’s certificate gives pneumonia and tuberculosis, not surgery, so the story of the arm surgery does not match either brother yet. It may be a memory that has blended with another family illness, and it is still an open question. Questions for the family Does anyone know Esther’s birth year, or the names of her grandchildren? Who was the brother who, in the family story, died after surgery on his arm? Does anyone know who “Mrs. Mary Awn” of Beirut was?

Grampian passenger list, Quebec, 3 September 1920: the Aoun family on lines 5 to 14, with “Uncle, Michal Malleut, Damour” as the nearest relative. From the record. Document 112 Nassib’s border card, 3 September 1920: age 22, travelling with “Youssouf, 53,” bound for Brooklyn “c/o Aunt.” From the record; the address is our reading. 25 Aug 1920 The family leaves Southampton on the Grampian 3 Sep 1920 The ship lands at Quebec 5 Sep 1920 Most of them cross into New York State at Rouses Point Then On to Brooklyn What we found Nassib’s own border card shows where the oldest son was headed: Brooklyn, in care of an aunt, at what looks like 202 Butler Street. The ship list names only an uncle back in Damour, so the card is the first sign of a relative on this side of the ocean (the address and the aunt’s name are our reading of faint writing). “Uncle, Michal Malleut, Damour” The S.S. Grampian passenger list, Quebec, 3 September 1920, the nearest relative named for the whole family On 25 August 1920 the Aoun family left Southampton on the S.S. Grampian, bound for Quebec, on third-class tickets. One of the small cards from that crossing, Anthony’s identification card, is still held by the family. It carries a doctor’s vaccination stamp, the words “U.S.A. Passenger,” and a hand-written “11” after the word “line” (our reading), which would be his line on the ship’s list. On the list, which was made out for the landing at Quebec on 3 September, the family stands together on lines 5 to 14. Joseph is written Youseuf, a farmer of 53 who could read Arabic. Assin is Essine, 45, “H’wife.” After them come Thirese (14), Georges (10), Michel (8), Elias (6) and Antoine (4), and then the older three: Nessil (22), Matilde (29) and Jean (16), whose calling is written “Carpenter.” Everyone’s last home is Damour, the destination is Brooklyn, and the nearest relative named for the whole party is an uncle, Michal Malleut, in Damour. No one in America is named. The list does not say how they were related; that the nine are Joseph and Assin’s children comes from the family and from the later records. From Quebec they went on by train. The naturalization papers of Anthony, Matilda, Mitchell, Theresa and John give 5 September 1920 for crossing into New York State at Rouses Point, and several name the Delaware & Hudson Railway. Elias’s papers give 7 September. Nassib’s border card then fills in a little more. It was filed on the same day as the ship list. It repeats the head-tax number from line 12, 5586, and it calls his nearest relative “Michel Mallout” of Damour, probably the same uncle spelled another way (our reading). It also says that his passage was paid by his parents (our reading). Not everything adds up. Anthony is 4 on the list but 6 by his own birth date, 6 March 1914. A 1940 Brooklyn Eagle story says that John came with “his father, mother, two sisters and four brothers,” but the list shows two sisters and five brothers besides John. Nassib died in 1924, which may be why a later writer counted four (we do not know). Still open The uncle: Michal Malleut is named for the whole family, and “Michel Mallout” on Nassib’s card is probably the same man. No record says who he was. The aunt: Nassib’s card says “c/o Aunt” and a name we cannot read, at an address that looks like 202 Butler Street, Brooklyn. We have not yet looked for that house in the 1920 and 1925 censuses. The ages: six of the nine children’s ages on the ship list do not match the 1925 census. Matilda is 29 on the list, 23 in the census, and born in 1899 by her own petition, so 20 on the ship. How many came: the Eagle’s count of four brothers against the list’s five. The day at Rouses Point: 5 September in five of the family’s papers, 7 September in Elias’s. Family memory: why they left Damour, what they carried, who met them in Brooklyn. If you know, please tell Sarah. Questions for the family Does anyone know who Michal Malleut, the uncle, was? Does anyone know who the aunt on Butler Street was? Did anyone hear why the family left Damour in 1920, or what the trip was like? Does anyone know what the family carried with them, or who met them in Brooklyn? How we know this Anthony’s 1920 identification card : third class, S.S. Grampian, from Southampton on 25 August 1920; vaccination stamp; a line number we read as 11. From the record. The name and the line number are our readings. The Grampian passenger list, Quebec, 3 September 1920 (National Archives M1464, List 1, sheet 46, lines 5 to 14): names and ages as printed, destination Brooklyn, nearest relative “Uncle, Michal Malleut, Damour.” From the record. Nassib’s Canadian border card, 3 September 1920 : age 22, head-tax number 5586, nearest relative “Michel Mallout,” bound for Brooklyn “c/o Aunt.” From the record. The relative’s name, the address and the aunt’s name are our readings. Canadian passenger-list index line for Elias, 1920 : age 6, arrived 3 September 1920 at Quebec on the Grampian. An index line, which points to the record but is not the record. Its “Brooklyn” as a birthplace is most likely the destination column misread. From the papers themselves.

A house full of working children By 1925 the family lived at 37 Tompkins Place in Brooklyn. The state census that year lists nine people at home, all born in Syria: Joseph, Assin and seven of their children. Nassib was missing, because he had died there the October before ( Confirmed : 1925 state census). By April 1930 Mathilde had married and moved out. John was a manager in a dry goods business, Theresa a clerk in dry goods, George a manager in ladies’ apparel and Mitchell a clerk ( Confirmed : 1930 census). The family says only Anthony and Mitchell were allowed to go to school while the others worked ( Family ). A graduate list of 1932 names an Anthony Aoun, who may be ours ( Probable ). 1924 Nassib dies at home 1925 Nine people under one roof 1926 Mathilde marries 1930 Several of the children are at work The details: records, spellings and open questions By 1925 the family was living at 37 Tompkins Place in Brooklyn. The New York State census taker wrote the name Owen and listed Joseph, Aseen (40), Matilda (23), John (21), Theresa (20), George (18), Micheal (16), Luis (13) and Anthony (10), all born in Syria ( Confirmed ). Nassib (Nessil) is missing because he had died the October before. Mathilde had married four years earlier and moved out. John (26) was a manager in a dry goods business, Theresa (23) a clerk in dry goods, George (21) a manager in ladies' apparel, Mitchell (20) a clerk, Elias (written Louis, 18) and Anthony (16) ( Confirmed ). The family was already in the clothing trade, which fits the family story that the brothers started with fabric and later ran the shop in Manhattan. Anthony probably finished high school in 1932. The Brooklyn Eagle of 30 June 1932 lists an Anthony Aoun among the Alexander Hamilton High School graduates ( Probable ; the list gives no address, so it is not certain this is him). The family says that only Anthony and Mitchell were allowed to go to school while the others worked ( Family ). Four brothers, one path The four brothers who settled in New York each became citizens between 1941 and 1943, and each followed the same steps: a declaration of intention, a petition, and an oath taken with two witnesses ( Confirmed : their naturalization papers). Mathilde took her oath on 30 June 1942. Theresa waited until 10 May 1955. Mitchell’s papers include a court order of 9 June 1943 that made Awn his legal name ( Confirmed ). Friends from Clinton Street, among them Said Owen, a shoemaker, stood as witnesses for several of the brothers. 6 Feb 1941 Elias becomes a citizen 30 Jun 1942 Mathilde becomes a citizen 5 Nov 1942 John becomes a citizen 10 Nov 1942 Anthony becomes a citizen 9 Jun 1943 Mitchell’s name is changed to Awn The details: records, spellings and open questions The brothers each took the same path to citizenship, and the papers survive: Elias : declaration of intention 1937; petition and oath with witnesses 1941. Mitchell : declaration 1939; WWII draft card 1940; petition; and a name-change order in 1943. John : declaration 1940; petition and oath with witnesses 1942. Anthony : declaration 1939; draft card 1940; petition and oath on 10 November 1942. See Part Three. t: The Saydah Family, from Forzul to Brooklyn
x: Helen's father, Antoon (W.) Saydah , came from Forzul , Lebanon. We call him Antoon, which is how the Arabic papers and his 1942 draft card write his first name; many records write it Anton, and some Antoun. His family name appears as Saydah, Saidah, Sayda, Saida and even Smyda. Helen's mother was born a Hadad (Wassela Hadad), a name that records also spell Hodod, Haddad and Hadel.

It is on his declaration of 1909 and again on his passport application of 1923 (as printed: “tatoo cross on left hand”). “tattoo cross (x) on left hand” Antoon’s declaration of intention, no. 9718, 9 November 1909 On 9 November 1909, in the Supreme Court of Kings County, a merchant named Antoon Wahbeh Saydah described himself for the clerk. He was 28, white, with a dark complexion, five feet six and 170 pounds, with black hair and brown eyes, and “tattoo cross (x) on left hand.” He lived at 570 48th Street, and he signed with an x before his name. In December 1923 he described himself again for a passport clerk, and the cross was still there. By those same sworn papers he was born in Forzul on 15 August 1881 and left Le Havre on the liner La Touraine about 17 October 1898, reaching New York on 25 October. We have not found his name on that sailing. The one line that may be him is on a La Touraine list marked as arriving on 28 November 1898: “Smyda, Antoun,” 18, single, a farmer who could read, from Beyrouth, with $20 and a “Brother, 73 W’g’ton St.” as his destination. A month apart and a spelling apart, it is not proven, and we treat it as a question for the family. If it is him, the brother is probably Khaleel, who lived at 73 Washington Street in 1900. The 1900 census finds an Anton Saydah, born 15 August 1880, aged 19 and single, a boarder in Abdalla Kirkish’s household in Negaunee, Michigan, “selling goods from house to house.” The Kirkish wife, Sady, is probably his sister Sada. By April 1910 he was back in Brooklyn, a single man of 29 in his brother Khaleel’s household at 570 48th Street, which is what proves that the two were brothers. His citizenship papers run from 1909 to 1914. On 8 May 1913 he petitioned as a merchant living at 5305 Sixth Avenue with his wife, Wassila. Two witnesses swore that they had known him in New York State since December 1905: Anton Simon, a commission merchant, and Willard Van Wagner, in dry goods. The petition also says “I have no children.” Their daughter Lily had been born and had died in March 1913, two months before, and we read the line as meaning living children. On 22 January 1914 he took the oath in open court, renouncing the Sultan of Turkey, and was handed certificate no. 381478, with the last digit written over. Written under it is a new address, 4721 Sixth Avenue. The directories and cards that follow show a working man. The 1913 Brooklyn directory lists him as “laces,” at 567 48th Street, the house where Khaleel, an importer, is listed too. On the draft card he signed on 12 September 1918 he is a manager at the Saydah Importer Co., 85 Washington Street, and his wife Wassela is his nearest relative. That card gives his birth as 15 August 1880, a year earlier than his own citizenship papers. In December 1923 he applied for a passport “for buying and manufacturing merchandise” for the Saydah Importing Co. across a long list of countries, from Portugal and Madeira to Egypt, Syria and Switzerland, naming his father, Wahbeh A. Saydah, as dead. He sailed on the Lapland on 16 January 1924 for about a year. The passenger lists let us follow part of the trip. On 11 July 1924 he was in Southampton as a first-class passenger on the Arundel Castle, with Madeira as the likely port of call (our reading of an abbreviation). On 4 August he came back to Southampton from Madeira on the Kildonan Castle. On 12 August he landed in New York from the Majestic, giving his home as 33 86th Street, Brooklyn. He had been gone about seven months, not a year. His name is also on the 1924 Brooklyn voter list, at 33 86th Street. The last of his own papers is the draft card of 1942, the “old man’s” registration for men born between 1877 and 1897. He was 61 by its count, living at 33 86th Street and still working for the Saydah Importing Co., at 236 Fifth Avenue. His wife “Wassella” is the person who will always know his address. He signed in English letters, with a handwritten note under the signature line that reads, as we read it, “arabic signature.” The back describes a man of five feet five and 180 pounds. Still open His birth year: his sworn papers of 1909, 1913 and 1923 say 15 August 1881. The 1900 census, his 1918 draft card and his manifest age of 18 say 1880. The 1942 card writes 1881 but gives an age of 61, which fits 1880. The day, 15 August, is the same in every record. His arrival: 25 October 1898 on his own papers, about September 1898 from Beirut on his passport application, 1900 on the 1930 census, and about 1901 on others. No Ellis Island search has found him, and the La Touraine line of 28 November is only a possible match. A baptism record from Forzul might settle this and his birth year. His certificate: certificate no. 381478 on his own papers, but the handwritten number 423396 beside his name on the 1924 Majestic list is unexplained. Forzul or Forgul: the cursive letter in his birthplace is not settled. Family memory: stories of the voyage, why he left, the cross on his hand, or the trip to Madeira. If you know, please tell Sarah. Questions for the family Does anyone know what took Antoon to Michigan, or who met him in New York? Did anyone hear stories of his voyage in 1898, or about the cross on his hand? What did he buy on the 1924 trip, and did he talk about Madeira? Does anyone know who Anton Simon and Willard Van Wagner, his 1913 witnesses, were? What we found Wassela’s family name is Hodod on her marriage certificate, Hadad in the 1900 census and Hadel in 1910. It is the same family ( Confirmed ). t: Wassela's family: the Hadads (Hodod) and the Shehadis
x: What we found Hanna Hadad died in upstate New York, yet he lies in a grave with no marker in Syracuse, and we do not yet know why ( Probable : Find a Grave). The Hadads of Zahle Wassela’s father, Hanna (John) Hadad, and her mother, Amina Shehadi, were both in America by 1892, according to the census. In 1900 the family was living on DeGraw Street in Brooklyn, in the household of Amina’s probable brother Beshara Shahady ( Confirmed : census; Probable for the brother). Wassela’s brothers Salim, Charles and Najib appear in the censuses. On New Year’s night 1913 a Salim Hadad was shot in the shoulder after a quarrel and sent home. The event is Confirmed ; that he is Wassela’s brother is Probable . That autumn Hanna, who had spent his last eighteen months at the Clifton Springs health resort, died on 11 October 1913 (where he died is an open conflict, see below), and the funeral was in Syracuse ( Confirmed : Syracuse Post-Standard). 1892 Both parents are in America 1900 DeGraw Street, Brooklyn 1913 Salim is shot, and Hanna dies The details: records, spellings and open questions The family name also appears as Hadad on Wassela’s daughter Evelyn’s Social Security record. Her mother’s maiden name, Shehadi , is also written Shahady. Her parents. Her father appears as John Hodod on her marriage certificate, but the Arabic papers, including the 1912 wedding notice, call him Hanna Haddad (Hanna is the Arabic form of John) and place his home at Mu’allaqa, Zahle ( Confirmed ). He was born about 1850 (the 1900 census says March 1850, and the 1910 census says age 65). In June 1900 he was out of work and had been for twelve months. Her mother, Amina (Shehadi was her family name), appears as Emmel in 1900 and Ameeny in 1910. She was born about 1865, and had borne eight children by 1900, five of whom were living, and nine by 1910, four of whom were living. The census says both parents came in 1892. An 1898 business directory (Trow's Brooklyn and Queens volume) lists a John Haddad, grocer, on Washington Street (the borough is not printed; probably Manhattan), who may be Wassela's father (a question for the family). The documents behind this 2 documents Document 96 1900 census, Degraw Street, Brooklyn: the Hadad family Document 97 Trow's Brooklyn directory for 1898: John Haddad, grocer Hanna’s last months, 1913. For the last eighteen months of his life Hanna was at the Clifton Springs health resort in upstate New York. He died there on Saturday 11 October 1913, at about 68 (the notices say 68, the 1910 census 65, Find a Grave 66 or 67). The day is Confirmed by the Syracuse Post-Standard of 13 October 1913, which says he died on Saturday (Find a Grave gives the same day but is only a pointer). The Post-Standard calls him John Hadad; that this John is Hanna is Probable , because the age, Clifton Springs, the Syracuse burial and the son-in-law Antoon Saydah in the Arabic notice all fit. Where he died is an open conflict: the Arabic notices and the Post-Standard say Clifton Springs, but the state’s death index lists the entry (certificate no. 50442) under “Willard.” The funeral was held on 13 October at the Church of the Savior, an Episcopal church in Syracuse, and he was buried in Oakwood Cemetery there, in Section H-2, plot 87, in a grave with no marker ( Probable : Find a Grave memorial 115947080). The Arabic notices name his widow Amina, his sons Salim, Khaleel and Najib, and his son-in-law Antoon Saydah of Brooklyn (Al-Hoda, 17 October 1913, page 3; Mira’at al-Gharb, 18 October 1913, page 5; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). Why he was buried in Syracuse, where the Shehadi family lived, rather than in Brooklyn we do not know. The documents behind this 2 documents Document 140 John Hadad dies at Clifton Springs (Syracuse), October 1913 Document 141 Hanna Haddad's death notice, Al-Hoda, 17 October 1913 The Shehadi cousins in Syracuse. The Arabic notice says Michael and Yusuf Shehadi, merchants in Syracuse, were Hanna’s “cousins.” The Post-Standard says he was the brother-in-law of Michel and Joseph Shehadi. Put together, Michel and Joseph are probably Amina’s brothers ( Probable ), and we keep both wordings. Her brothers. The 1900 census at Deep River lists a jeweler written “William Sayydah” with a wife, Mary, and sons Ferris and Harold, and Cecil’s delayed birth certificate of 1940 calls his father Murad a “watch maker” at Deep River in 1901. We think these are all one man, Antoon’s brother Murad. The name, the town, the trade and the family all fit, but no record says it in so many words. Murad was alive in January 1920. That month’s census finds him in Oak Park, Illinois, head of the household, in the “jewelry” trade with his “own store.” He was probably dead by June 1925, when Tirkman heads her own household in the census; we do not know the date or place of his death. What the records show is his widow, Tirkman (born Abu Ayn, the Arabic papers say; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader), and her children Fares (written Ferris on his marriage certificate), Harold and Cecil, and Nora, who died in 1920. Nora’s death certificate of 29 May 1920 names her father as Murad Saydah. In 1926 Tirkman gave to the Zahle Relief Committee, a fund for the homeland, and in May 1927 an Arabic paper listed a Mrs. Tirkman Saydah among the Syrian women sailing to Lebanon that week. It is probably Tirkman, but whether she went, and who went with her, is not shown. Then the records turn. Four days after the Oak Park census taker counted Murad at home, a census taker at the Chicago State Hospital for the Insane at Norwood Park, Illinois, wrote down an inmate named “Sayyidah Murad,” male, 48, married, born in Syria, with no occupation. That is the page as printed, dated 6 January 1920. Ten years earlier, on 4 May 1910, a “Patient” named “Sayyidah Murad,” 39, born in Syria and in the United States since 1890, was listed at the Cook County Hospital for Insane at the same place. The name, the age, Syria and 1890 all fit our Murad. We do not know what to make of the January 1920 pair. It may be two men, one man counted twice (at home by his family and in the hospital), or one entry put in the wrong place, and we have not settled it. If Murad was a patient, the hospital’s own admission, discharge or death registers might say when and where he died, and we have not yet found them. Tirkman died on Saturday 7 September 1929, aged 51, at St. Mary’s Hospital in Brooklyn. Al-Hoda of 9 September, the Brooklyn Daily Times of 10 September and her death certificate call her the widow of Murad Saydah. Her death notice calls her the wife of the brother of Khaleel, Michael and Antoon (as printed in Arabic; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). We take the Antoon named to be Antoon Saydah, Helen’s father, which is why we place Murad among Antoon’s brothers. Michael’s own death notice of 1953 counts Murad among his late brothers (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). Her son Fares married Alice Awad on 18 December 1926 at the Union Church of Bay Ridge (marriage certificate no. 18195); the Arabic notice had announced the wedding for 11 December, and the certificate settles the day as 18 December. Fares died on 3 October 1942 at Presbyterian Hospital in Manhattan, and his death certificate, no. 19540, gives his home as Tenafly, New Jersey. Two families from two Lebanese villages came together in Brooklyn at the end of 1940. They did not have far to go to find each other. The Awn brothers lived at 1047 Bay Ridge Parkway, which is 75th Street, and the Saydahs at 33 86th Street, about eleven blocks away in the same Brooklyn neighborhood of Bay Ridge. We do not yet know how Anthony and Helen met, and it is a good question for the family.

Awn was born on 6 March 1914 in Damour and arrived at six as Antoine Aoun. He filed his declaration of intention in 1939 and registered for the draft on 16 October 1940. The draft card names his employer as Koury-Awn, Inc. , at 38 East 32nd Street, and gives his brother John at 1047 Bay Ridge Parkway as the person to contact. Mitchell's draft card, written the same day, names a different employer, his brother John at 82 Greenwich Street, so the East 32nd Street firm and the Greenwich Street shop were separate businesses in 1940. He took the oath of citizenship on 10 November 1942 . His petition describes him as 5 feet 8½ inches tall and 172 pounds, living at 123 Marine Avenue, with a wife, Helen (born 9 January 1917 in Brooklyn), a son, Joseph (born 14 November 1941), and a request to be known as Anthony Awn. Part of good research is knowing which records are not ours. These are written down so nobody has to search for them twice. Joseph Owen, who died 27 April 1932 at 385 Clinton Street, is not Anthony's father. His death certificate (no. 9788) calls him a grocer of 55 whose wife was Sadie and whose parents were Michael and Mary, and says he had lived in the U.S. 18 years. Joseph (Anthony's father) died in September 1932, aged 62, married to Assin, with parents Peter and Teresa. The same cemetery (St. John's) and the same undertaker (Jere J. Cronin, Inc.) buried both, but Owen was a common spelling among Brooklyn Syrian families and nothing ties the two men together ( Confirmed : a different man, since the ages, wives, parents and addresses differ). A "John Khouri" fruit-store lead is not John Awn ( Family , from Sarah). A 1906 petition by a Salim Haddad (born 1883, in the U.S. since 1900, living on Washington Street in Manhattan) and a 1897 Kansas City card for a Salim Hadad are Probably different men from Wassela's brother Salim, who was in Brooklyn by 1892 and in the June 1900 census. The January 1898 ship card for ten-year-old "Wassilah Hadad" Probably describes a different girl, because the Hadads were already living in Brooklyn. The 1920 Ishpeming census page for an Assad Kirkish household (pictured in item 106) is probably a different Kirkish family. Assad's wife Sadie could be the "Sada Kirkish" named in the 1953 Eagle notice, so it stays open as a question for the family. George Abraham Saydah of Bay Ridge is not shown to be related. His 1923 declaration says he was born on 15 October 1880 (his 1926 petition says 1882), sailed from Naples on the Prinzess Irene and reached New York on 29 or 30 August 1906 (last foreign residence Cairo), and lived on Ovington Avenue in Brooklyn, with wife Melia and three children born in Hoboken. His petition is no. 68097. Nothing in the papers names Antoon, Khaleel or Michael, so he stays here until a record links him (a link is only a question for the family; FamilySearch, Brooklyn naturalizations, NARA image group 007784999, images 703, 705 and 706 of 1018). Antone Saddy, a 22-year-old Syrian lodger in the 1920 Manhattan census (sheet 10A, enumeration district 1421; FamilySearch ark 3:1:33SQ-GRNV-WRQ, image 1127 of 1176) is Probably a different man, since Antoon Saydah was in Brooklyn with his wife and daughter in January 1920. “Ambassador George Hakim,” Lebanon’s representative to the United Nations, on the front page of The Caravan, 22 June 1961, is Probably not George Michael Hakim, the husband of Virginia. Virginia's husband George was a Brooklyn man, a Columbia graduate and an Army staff sergeant in 1945, and later a marketing executive in New Jersey. Nothing on the page mentions Brooklyn or the Saydah or Awn families, and Hakim is a common Lebanese name (Brooklyn Newsstand, Caravan, 22 June 1961, page 1). A Social Security index entry for “V Hakim,” born 1925 and died 2006, last living in New York, is not Virginia Saydah Hakim. Her obituary says she was born in 1921 and died on 26 August 2015, which is after that index entry’s date and does not match it (Social Security Death Index; obituary in The Record, 27 August 2015).

A family history is never finished. These are the open questions. If you know anything about any of them, please use the sharing form below. Anthony and Helen’s wedding. The date, Sunday 29 December 1940, comes from two Arabic papers and Anthony’s petition; a Caravan anniversary note of 1958 gives 28 December, so we would still like the marriage certificate, which would also confirm the church (both papers print St. Anselm’s). George Awn. He drowned on 27 July 1930. We do not know where (Long Island or a lake in Rhode Island), why his age is given as 24, 22 and 21, or who the friend with him was. A death record or the New York papers of 28 and 29 July 1930 would settle it. Anthony’s death certificate and Wassela’s 1969 death record. We have Anthony’s death notice (Home Reporter, 15 July 1966) but not his certificate. For Wassela there is a newspaper index entry (The Record of Hackensack, 8 January 1969) and a sympathy notice, but not the certificate. Birth years. Was Antoon born in 1880 or 1881? And when was Wassela born? The 1900 census says 1886, while every later record says about 1889 to 1893. Is Zahleh really her birthplace? A second record for each would settle it. The church. Anthony’s side was Maronite, at Our Lady of Lebanon. The notices say the bride was not Maronite, and the Saydahs used Presbyterian and Episcopal churches (Khaleel studied at a Presbyterian seminary, and Antoon’s funeral was at Christ Episcopal), so they look Protestant ( Probable ). Our Lady of Lebanon’s registers may say more. Lebanon. We have not yet found records from Damour or Forzul. Parish and civil registers there could take us back past Joseph and Antoon. Koury-Awn, Inc., at 38 East 32nd Street, was Anthony's employer in 1940. We would like to know who ran it, and whether Michael Koury (Theresa's husband) was in the clothing business. Esther Ayoub's family in Beirut. The 1961 Caravan notice names her son Antoine Ayoub (with his wife and children) and her daughters Mrs. Sira San Remi and Mrs. Mary Awn of Beirut. It does not name a husband. Does anyone remember them? The Tuxedo Park accident, 1916. Who was driving, Antoon or Khaleel? And how did the new trial of 1919 end? We would like Najib Maloof’s death record and the court file. 73 Washington Street, 1898. The La Touraine entry for "Antoun Smyda" (if it is Antoon) says he was joining a brother at 73 Washington Street. That brother is Probably Khaleel, but we have not shown where Khaleel lived in 1898. A grocer named John Haddad is listed at 73 Washington Street in an 1898 directory, who may be Wassela's father (a question for the family). Did the two families share the address? Antoon's ship and arrival date. He swore he arrived on La Touraine on 25 October 1898. The only matching entry we found, "Antoun Smyda," 18, is on a La Touraine list dated 28 November 1898, and it may not be him. The year 1898 is supported by the 1900 and 1910 censuses, but his own name has not turned up on the 25 October sailing. We need that page, or a record that confirms or rules out the Smyda entry. More open conflicts. Where Hanna Hadad died (Clifton Springs or “Willard”), where Antoon died (Allendale or Columbia, South Carolina), which church held Joseph’s funeral (St. Mary’s or Our Lady of Lebanon), who Sa’da Kirkish’s husband was (the 1953 notice puts both sisters in California; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader), and who the Najeeb Hadad of 4721 Sixth Avenue (died 13 January 1914) was. Other records also disagree: Michael’s house number on Fort Hamilton Parkway (8646 in the 1953 Eagle and Arabic notices, 8726 elsewhere); Joseph’s birth (his 1932 certificate prints 21 November 1869, but its age of 62 years, 9 months and 7 days fits about 7 December 1869); Khaleel’s birth (about 1868 in the 1900 and 1905 censuses, 19 March 1870 on his death certificate); and Virginia’s birth (29 June 1921 in her obituary, about December 1921 by the 1930 census). Fred Gorayeb's death, and where he and Mathilde are buried. Mathilde Probably died in December 1984, from an index entry. We have found nothing on Fred's death. Murad Saydah, and his widow Tirkman’s family. We have no record of when or where Murad died. He was alive in January 1920 and probably dead by June 1925, and Tirkman’s 1929 obituary calls her his widow, so the years to search are 1920 to 1925. Also open: the day of Tirkman’s funeral (Tuesday 10 September 1929 in the Arabic notice, “to-morrow” in the Brooklyn Daily Times of that day; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader) and her parents (Abdo Bouinain and Sylvia Bouman (as we read the hand) on her certificate, the Abu Ayn family in the Arabic papers); the wedding day of Fares and Alice (18 December 1926 on the certificate, 11 December in the Arabic notice); and Ferris’s birth day (2 or 26 February 1896) and death place (Manhattan in the New York City index, Tenafly where he lived). Sada and Nustas Kirkish. The 1948, 1949 and 1953 notices for Khaleel, Antoon and Michael all name them as sisters. Sada is Probably "Sady," wife of Abdalla Kirkish, in whose Michigan household Antoon boarded in 1900. We have not yet found a record naming their parents. Michigan death certificates and the Kirkish censuses might. Evelyn and Virginia in 1940. The 1940 census page we found lists only Antoon, Wassela and Helen, and the next sheet has not been checked. The sisters' marriages are known from newspapers and indexes (Virginia in 1945, Evelyn in 1954 and 1971), but we have not seen the marriage certificates. Michael Saydah. Antoon's brother Michael lived in Chicago from about 1891 and was in Brooklyn by December 1919 ( Confirmed : his son Victor's death certificate, 31 December 1919, at 570 48th Street, item 58); when he moved is not yet shown. He died on 1 March 1953 ( Confirmed : his death notice in the Brooklyn Eagle of 3 March 1953) and was buried in Green-Wood Cemetery on 4 March. We do not know what became of his first wife, Marie Luckey (married in Grundy County, Illinois, in 1901), or whether he was born in 1877, as his own records say, or about 1870, as his sons' certificates imply. His 1903 naturalization is known only from his own sworn statements in the 1917 and 1922 passport applications; we have not seen the certificate, and the Cook County papers may name his parents. Mitchell Awn's two wives, Barbara Machanskis and Laurdes Nassr, and what became of Barbara. Living memories. A conversation with family would fill in what no record keeps, such as Esther Ayoub's family and which brother had the arm surgery.

Joseph's death certificate, 14 September 1932. The New York City certificate for "Joseph K. Owen," died at about 1 a.m. on 14 September 1932 in Brooklyn, born 21 November 1869, aged 62 years, 9 months, 7 days (this day count does not fit the printed birth date: from 21 November 1869 to 14 September 1932 is 62 years, 9 months and 24 days, while 9 months and 7 days would point to about 7 December 1869, so the records disagree and his birth date is an open question). It lists him as married to "Assin Owen," retired, 12 years in the U.S. and in New York City, son of "Peter Owen" and "Teresa Owen," both of Syria. The cause is cardiac failure (one day), with coronary thrombosis (six days) contributing, signed by the attending physician. Burial was at St. John's Cemetery on 16 September, with Jere J. Cronin, Inc., of 115 Atlantic Avenue as undertaker. The second picture is the bottom of the back of the certificate, where the undertaker's statement is signed "Mrs. Assin Owen" as the "Wife" of the deceased, the person who asked for the burial permit. Assin's death certificate, 16 October 1935. The certificate for "Assin Owen," a widow aged 52 who did housework, died about 1 a.m. on 16 October 1935 at Bay Ridge Hospital, Brooklyn; she lived at 1047 75th Street and had been in the U.S. and New York City for 14 years. Her date of birth is blank. The cause is acute gangrenous appendicitis (ruptured), after an appendectomy, with toxic myocarditis contributing. She was buried at St. John's Cemetery on 18 October. Joseph's death notice, September 1932. As printed: Joseph K. Owen, 62, of 590 78th Street, died "yesterday" at home. He was born in Damour, Syria, and had lived in Brooklyn for 12 years. He leaves his wife, Affin (Assin); four sons, John, Mitchell, Louis and Anthony; and two daughters, Matilda and Theresa. The funeral was to go from the home to St. Mary's Syrian R. C. Church on Hicks Street for a requiem mass, with burial at St. John's Cemetery under J. J. Cronin. Four things stand out. Louis is Elias, who signed his 1937 marriage certificate as Louis J. Awn. The same four sons are named in Esther Ayoub’s 1961 notice. George, who was 21 in the April 1930 census, is named in none of the three notices, and neither is Nassib (Nessil), who died in 1924; we now know why. George drowned in July 1930, from the Arabic papers of that week and Nassib died in 1924. The address, 590 78th Street, is also the address on Joseph's death certificate (item 82), while the 1930 Arabic notice for George (item 135) gives 466 78th Street. And the funeral church is St. Mary’s Syrian Roman Catholic, while the Arabic papers say Our Lady of Lebanon, so that detail is still open. Source: Brooklyn Times Union, 15 September 1932, page 22 (taken from the file name of the saved copy; the clipping itself does not print the paper or date). Names as printed: Joseph K. Owen, Affin, John, Mitchell, Louis, Anthony, Matilda, Theresa.

t: Document 141: Hanna Haddad's death notice, Al-Hoda, 17 October 1913

The address of his home in Brooklyn is given as 4721 Sixth Avenue . This is the Arabic notice that names Antoon as his son-in-law. It does not say "John"; that the "John" of the English papers (item 140) is Hanna is Probable , because the age (68), Clifton Springs, the Syracuse burial and the son-in-law Saydah all fit. 4721 Sixth Avenue is also the address on Najeeb Hadad's 1914 death record, which fits Najeeb living in this household; that is only a lead. t: Document 139: Salim Hadad is shot (Arabic), 2 January 1913

One of them fired a pistol and hit Haddad's shoulder, wounding him lightly. The police arrested one of them and his companion Mansour ran away. This agrees with the English report (item 138) on the event, the wound and the arrest, but the details differ: the English paper names one other man (of 324 Livingston Street) and puts the shooting at the corner of Atlantic Avenue and Henry Street, while the Arabic names two men (Mansour Abdo and Michel, whose surname is hard to read) and says it happened in Salim's shop. Murad’s widow. She gave to the Zahle Relief Committee in 1926 and was listed among the women sailing to the homeland in May 1927 (an Arabic paper; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). Tirkman, born Abu Ayn according to the Arabic papers (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader); Tikam (1925 census); Tirkman Bouanain (Cecil’s Iowa delayed birth record); Saydah (death certificate). The certificate names her parents as Abdo Bouinain and Sylvia Bouman (as we read the hand), while the Arabic papers say Abu Ayn, an open conflict; Nora’s 1920 certificate gives the mother’s maiden name as Mary Boainam Born About 1878, Syria (age 51 in 1929; 42 in 1920; 48 in 1925) Died 7 September 1929, aged 51, St. Mary’s Hospital, Brooklyn; buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery on 10 September; she lived at 39 Gelston Avenue Funeral day The Arabic paper announced Tuesday 10 September 1929 (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader); the Brooklyn Daily Times printed “to-morrow” on 10 September, so the day is an open conflict Spouse Murad Saydah Children Fares (Ferris), Harold and Cecil, and a daughter, Nora, who died on 29 May 1920 Listed among the women sailing, May 1927 Arabic paper (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader).
